verdicts.claim: 1. A closed op tree with two owners per op can express the derived columns analysts reach for, so v1 needs no expression-string or code escape hatch.
verdicts.reason: The no-escape-hatch half holds (it is the only way why(), serialization and the SQL owner survive, and the grammars lens confirms it). The vocabulary half does not: the listed ops miss string membership (contains/startsWith/in), a days-between two dates (the single most common date derivation), percent-of-total (an aggregate with an EMPTY groupBy — the design only allows aggregates 'over a group'), and any cross-table lookup. The date ops are also under-declared: the demo's own time axis is MMWR week (vizfootprint-demo/src/nndss/etl.ts:19,82 — week 1 contains Jan 4, Sunday–Saturday), while `week` on ISO strings would silently mean ISO week — a derived `week` column would then disagree with the source's `week` column with no sentence explaining why. Finally 'two owners per op' hides semantic drift the conformance table must pin: JS `Math.round` (half away from zero) vs DuckDB ROUND (half to even), `%` sign on negatives, integer vs float division, string case rules, date parsing of non-ISO text.
verdicts.fix: Add `contains/startsWith/endsWith/in`, `daysBetween(a,b)`, allow `over: { groupBy: [] }` for grand totals; make every date op carry its calendar as data (`week(t, 'iso' | 'mmwr')`, `dayOfWeek` with a stated first day); write the per-op absence rule AND the rounding/sign/division rule beside each op row, and make the conformance fixture include a negative modulus, a .5 rounding, an integer division and a non-ISO date so the fold and the SQL owner are proven to agree or the op is refused on that engine with `derive-unsupported-on-engine`.

verdicts.claim: 2. materializeColumn plus branch-scoped visibility through the fold is a sufficient landing spot for derived columns, so no new storage path is needed in the memory engine.
verdicts.reason: Four properties of the door break the honesty law. (a) It is name-keyed and in-place (memoryProvider.ts materializeColumn: `store.columns[name] = [...values]` / `r[name] = values[i]`) and cannot un-materialize (session.ts:1186-1199 says so): two branches declaring the SAME field with DIFFERENT trees share one physical column, so branch B silently reads branch A's numbers — a derived column whose values its own declaring commit cannot explain. (b) Editing a formula on one branch (a second `column` commit on the same field) overwrites the values in place, but the table version does not move, so every earlier commit on that branch that filtered on the old values (stamped `data: {table: X}`) is now irreproducible and `dataMoved` (ui/src/adapter/sessionView.ts:579) will NOT mark it — a silent misdating. (c) `materializeColumn` ends with `store.columnTypes[name] = inferType(values)` — the TypeTally rule re-types the column, overriding the design's 'typed by construction from the op table'; an all-absent derived column becomes `unknown`, and the header would then show a tally that contradicts the declaration. (d) Values are positional against 'the table's existing row order' with no version on the landed column, so a landing that races a refresh (refresh replaces the provider, buildDashboard.ts:302) can misalign by one whole row set.
verdicts.fix: Keep the door but give it identity and a version: land under a physical address `${field}@${declaringCommitId}` (or a content address `hash(tree, input addresses, table version)`), let the session fold map `field → address` per branch, and extend the CommitRecord `data` stamp (or a sibling `derived` stamp) with the addresses of every derived column visible at the cursor, so `dataMoved` can name 'formula of ratio changed' exactly as it names a moved table version. Add `materializeColumn(table, name, values, { type, version })` so the declared type wins and a version mismatch is a typed rejection (`version-moved`), never a positional misalignment.

verdicts.claim: 3. Re-deriving declared columns automatically after a refresh is always safe and cheap enough to run in the normal tier, because a declaration can be re-run where an analysis output cannot.
verdicts.reason: 'Re-runnable' is true and is the right distinction from `materialisedLost`. 'Always safe' is not: (a) the store is shared across branches (refresh swaps in ONE fresh provider, buildDashboard.ts:302), so 'the declared columns' means declarations on EVERY branch including archived ones — the design does not say whether re-derivation is all-branches-eager or cursor-lazy, and the answer decides which columns silently hold stale values on a branch switch; (b) a derived column that reads an analysis-materialised column (cluster_id) loses its input on refresh (`materialisedLost`) — `derive-input-missing` covers it, but the session's `allMaterialized` set (session.ts:494) keeps the dead name, so the gap sentence would name a column the engine no longer lists; (c) under ruling 12 every stage output is a footprintjs commit — committing a 1M-value column per stage means a structuredClone per commit (commitValues 'full'), so a chain of five columns at 1M rows is five 1M-element clones per refresh, well over the 2,000 ms silent threshold on the bench's numbers (columnar fold alone is 110 ms at 1M); (d) the default-table-only `stampData` (session.ts:518) means a re-derivation on a non-default table cannot even be dated.
verdicts.fix: Rule: re-derive lazily per branch on cursor arrival (what the fold makes visible), eagerly only for the cursor's branch, and record each re-derivation in the journal with the branch tip it served. In the flowchart, commit a column HANDLE (address, version, rowCount, absentCount) as the stage output and keep values in the store — sliceForKey slices by key, so handles preserve why(). Prune `allMaterialized` entries named in `materialisedLost`. Stamp `data` with every table the commit names (the column's table plus input tables), not just the default table.

verdicts.claim: 4. One column verb with slots (formula/label/type/role/scale/unit, null = back to the declaration) covers derivation, rename, type fix and drop without a second declaration surface.
verdicts.reason: One verb, one fold key, the prose/link `null` rule and the proposal lane are all sound reuse. Three holes: (a) `formula: null` is overloaded — on a source-less field it means DROP, but on a field declared in `DataSourceDef.derived` it means 'back to the def's tree', so a def-declared derived column can never be dropped in a session; (b) the `type` slot on a derived column contradicts 'typed by construction' — which wins, and does a declared type that disagrees with the tree's computed type refuse or coerce? (c) `role: 'absence'` through this verb would re-open the absence vocabulary, which section 3 rules a dashboard act — the verb must refuse that value. Also the fold key `column:<table>.<field>:<slot>` embeds `.` and `:` as delimiters while field names are free strings (the demo has `report_state`; a CSV header can carry a dot), and `unit` is a facet `ColumnFacet` does not have today.
verdicts.fix: Add an explicit `drop: true` (or slot `present: false`) distinct from `null`; state that `type` on a derived column is refused with `derive-invalid` ('its type is computed: number — declare a cast in the formula instead'); refuse `role: 'absence'` with a sentence pointing at the def; carry `{table, field}` as structured fields on the commit (viewId `column:` + a JSON-safe id) instead of a dotted string; add `unit` to `ColumnFacet` and `whats_here` in the same packet.

verdicts.claim: 5. Sheet arrangement as navigate commits on the layout identity, with widths and scroll excluded, keeps the log free of noise while making a beat's sheet screenshot reproducible.
verdicts.reason: LY-1 is a real precedent (session.ts:2019-2062) and it is the right home, but its guard accepts only a PLAIN STRING value capped at LAYOUT_VALUE_MAX = 500 characters (session.ts:201, :2049). A hidden-column list or a column order for a 30-column table can exceed 500 characters, and sort needs an encoded string (`field:dir`) — each prop needs a declared, documented string grammar or the guard rejects it with `guard-failed`. 'Reproducible screenshot' is also over-claimed: with widths per-viewer, wrapped labels, truncation and the visible row window differ between viewers; what the log reproduces is the same rows, columns, order and sort — not pixels. Widths excluded is the right call, but the beat should say what it reproduces.
verdicts.fix: Widen `doLayoutNote` for the sheet scope to accept a JSON-safe value (or raise the cap and document a grammar per prop: `sort=field:asc`, `hidden=a,b,c`, `order=…`, `frozen=2`), one `navigate` per prop, last-wins; document in the beat that a sheet beat reproduces the rectangle contract (rows/columns/sort/first visible row), and let the story bridge quote that rectangle rather than promising a pixel match.

verdicts.claim: 6. Header stats from one foldOnce over all rows per data version are affordable at 90k and 1M rows without sampling, so the Sampled badge will rarely appear.
verdicts.reason: Step 0 already measured this (bench/step0/REPORT.md): a 4-recorder fold is 3.7 ms at 90k and 28 ms at 1M; the all-column `columnar+columnTypes` fold is 22.8 ms at 90k and 110 ms at 1M for 13 columns. A profile with extent+distinct+groupCount+types+absence over 30 columns therefore lands around 50–80 ms at 90k (fine, once per version) and several hundred ms at 1M — over the 50 ms line but under the 2,000 ms silent threshold, so 'affordable once per version in the normal tier' holds. What does not hold is memory: `distinct` (fold.ts:91) keeps every value in a Set, so a unique-id column at 1M rows is a 1M-entry Set per such column (the bench's unique keyedIndex was 56–65 ms and the slowest fold), and 30 columns of high-cardinality strings multiply it. The badge will rarely appear only because the design has no exactness cap on distinct — it would instead blow memory silently.
verdicts.fix: Give the profile's `distinct` a declared cap (`distinctCap`, placeholder 10,000): exact up to the cap, then `{ count: 'over', atLeast: cap }` — an honest 'more than 10,000 distinct' shown in the header, never a sample. Keep `groupCount` top-k the same way. Add measurement 1 to step 0 as 'profile over ALL 13 real columns at 90k and 1M with the cap', and let the Sampled badge remain reserved for a scheduler-bounded walk.

verdicts.claim: 7. The sheet's per-window ViewQuery (limit/offset/sort in rows mode plus count mode) is exactly the rectangle contract every grid needs, so vendor adapters stay thin.
verdicts.reason: The rectangle shape matches every grid the lens surveyed and count mode exists today (memoryProvider evaluate `mode: 'count'`). But `evaluate` has `limit` and `columns` and NO `sort` or `offset` (types.ts EvaluateOptions; the bench notes 'a page at offset 5,000 materializes all matches then slices'), so both are new. The thinness claim breaks on FILTER, not on the rectangle: a vendor grid's header filter (AG Grid filterModel: contains / startsWith / blank / number ranges) is richer than the clause vocabulary (`point | interval | cell | match` — types.ts and log.ts:61), so an adapter must either invent predicates the port cannot express or drop them silently.
verdicts.fix: Add `sort` and `offset` to the view-query port with `sort` as `[{field, dir}]` (multi-column, as every sortModel is); declare on `SheetData.capabilities.filter` exactly which clause kinds are honoured, and make every adapter map an unsupported filterModel entry to a typed refusal `sheet-unsupported` shown in the header (never a silent no-op) — the conformance fixture should include one unsupported vendor filter and assert the refusal.

verdicts.claim: 8. A cached sorted index per (sort, filter, version) epoch makes sort at 1M rows a one-time cost rather than a per-window cost.
verdicts.reason: Cost model is right (one sort, then O(1) slices — the bench shows slicing an already-materialised answer is 0.00 ms). The KEY is insufficient for a provenance-first engine: a sort on a derived column whose formula was edited (a new `column` commit on the same field, same table version) must invalidate the index, and so must a branch switch that changes which derived values are visible — the table `version` moves for neither. Also 'filter' here must be the filter as evaluated for the sheet (own clause excluded, link responses applied), not the raw activeFilters map, or two identical-looking keys serve different rectangles.
verdicts.fix: Key the index on `(sort, canonical filter clauses for this view, table version, address of every derived column referenced by sort or filter)` — with the physical addresses from the fix to claim 2 this is exact; keep one LRU of a few indices per table and evict on refresh.

verdicts.claim: 9. DOM virtualization is enough at 90k rows and acceptable at 1M for 30 columns, so canvas is not needed in v1.
verdicts.reason: Step 0 has no browser rendering numbers at all (its REPORT says React render and main-thread contention 'are not in these numbers'; bench/x4 is the browser harness). The grids lens supports DOM at 90k on AG Grid's own statements, and canvas forfeits the accessibility tree, so the direction is right — but at 1M × 30 columns the risk is COLUMN virtualisation and per-frame DOM churn, which nobody has measured here. Not a provenance issue; simply unmeasured.
verdicts.fix: Keep measurement 7 as the gate and make it a real-Chromium x4 run (frame time while scrolling 30 columns, time-to-first-paint at 1M, DOM node count); only then decide `renderer: dom | canvas`.

verdicts.claim: 10. selectedRows' filter as the first view-query customer and the sheet as the second is the lower-risk order and the two counts will match byte for byte.
verdicts.reason: The ordering is right (selectedRows is a refactor with no UI). 'Byte for byte' is false in general: `Overview.selectedRowCount` is `selectedCount(defaultTable, [...activeFilters.values()])` — EVERY view's clause on the DEFAULT table, with no self-exclusion and no link responses (session.ts:2519, :1216-1224); the session never consults the link graph for engine counts (edgesInto is used only for encoding follow, :1881). The sheet as designed excludes its own clause (a row click must not filter the sheet to one row), honours `highlight` vs `filter` per edge, and may live on a non-default table. The two counts agree only when the sheet has no own selection, every edge into it is `filter`, and it shows the default table.
verdicts.fix: State the parity oracle precisely: `sheet.count()` with no own clause and all-filter edges on the default table equals `Overview.selectedRowCount`; add a second oracle for the general case by giving the session ONE function `clausesFor(viewId)` (own clause excluded, link responses applied) that both the sheet and a future per-view `selectedRowCount(viewId)` call — so the engine, not the UI, owns which clauses reach a view.

verdicts.claim: 11. Aggregate-kind derived columns over a groupBy cover most of what analysts would otherwise need a join for, so leaving joins out of v1 costs little.
verdicts.reason: The design's own first live derivation refutes it: `cases_per_100k` needs population, and the NNDSS cells table has no population column (etl.ts CellRow: jurisdiction, kind, disease, week_index, year, week, t, cases, report_state, flag, ytd, ytd_state, prev52_max; def.ts data = cells, jurisdictions, series; data/geo holds only the state outlines). Population is a lookup from another table by jurisdiction — a join in all but name. Worse for the aggregate substitute: the cells table contains region and total ROLL-UP rows as ordinary rows (kind: state | region | total), so `sum(cases) over disease` double-counts unless the aggregate can exclude rows — and the design's aggregate has no `where`. So the aggregate kind neither replaces the lookup nor is safe on the very table the demo uses.
verdicts.fix: Add a `lookup` op in v1 — `{ op: 'lookup', args: [{ col: 'jurisdiction' }], from: { table: 'population', key: 'jurisdiction', value: 'pop' } }` — a declared, one-to-one, non-fanning cross-table read with a typed refusal `derive-lookup-not-unique` when the foreign key is not unique (Weave's key namespace as the precedent, not a join), so `cases_per_100k` is expressible without a grain change; give the aggregate kind an optional `over.where: Expr` (a row predicate over the same table, e.g. kind = 'state') and print it in the why sentence; keep true joins out until the grain ruling.

verdicts.claim: 12. A refresh as a journal event beside the log (not a commit) is the honest model because refreshed rows are visible to every session regardless of branch.
verdicts.reason: Code confirms the premise: refresh swaps one provider for the whole dashboard (buildDashboard.ts:302, `providers.set(table, fresh)`) and every session reads it through `providerFor` (:397); commits keep stamping `CommitRecord.data` (log.ts:85-90) and the ui derives `dataMoved` by comparing that stamp with the current source version (sessionView.ts:579) — so a refresh already cannot be a branch-scoped commit without lying about scope, and the ref-event journal (RESEARCH_STATE.md:100, :323) is the established home for cause-tagged non-commits. Two caveats to write down rather than refute: seek before a refresh can never restore the old rows (dataMoved is the honest label, not a restore), and the journal must persist beside the log or a replayed session loses the cause of every version move.
verdicts.fix: Add to the journal entry the branch tips that were re-derived (see claim 3) and persist the journal with the log export; note explicitly on the Sources tab that time travel across a refresh is labelled, not restored.

verdicts.claim: 13. Column lineage written from the tree at declaration in the OpenLineage shape is complete and needs no post-hoc parsing of SQL.
verdicts.reason: For source-column inputs the tree is complete, and never parsing SQL back is right (dbt's admitted gap). It is incomplete in three places the honesty law cares about: (a) an input that is itself an analysis-materialised column (cluster_id) has no source column — its lineage edge must point at the ANALYSIS commit or why() stops at a name; (b) `over.groupBy` columns are INDIRECT/GROUP_BY inputs and (if `where` is added) predicate columns are INDIRECT/FILTER inputs — the design lists only the tree's column refs; (c) the dataset-level input (the table version the column was derived against, and after re-derivation the new version) is not in the column-lineage facet, yet it is the part a non-programmer asks about ('which data?').
verdicts.fix: Write `inputFields` with `transformation.subtype` per role — IDENTITY/TRANSFORMATION for tree refs, GROUP_BY for `over.groupBy`, FILTER for `over.where`, and a `basis: { kind: 'analysis', commitId }` for materialised inputs — plus a dataset-level `derivedAgainst: { table, version }` that the journal's re-derivation entry updates; the why resolver for `kind: 'column'` reads these instead of scanning the log.

verdicts.claim: 14. A generated why-sentence from the tree plus the version stamp answers the questions a non-programmer asks of a column better than a formula or Excel-style arrows.
verdicts.reason: Better than arrows is well supported (arrows name cells, not steps or versions). 'Better than a formula for non-programmers' overreaches the cited evidence: Wrangler's non-programmers 'relied almost entirely on the previews', not on the sentences — the preview (example rows with inputs beside outputs) was the thing that worked. Two mechanics also undercut the sentence as drafted: '1,204 rows absent (population absent)' requires a per-INPUT absence tally, but the recorder as specified only counts absent RESULTS; and a sentence generated from a nested tree (an `if` inside a `div` inside a `coalesce`) becomes a clause chain nobody can read.
verdicts.fix: Pair the sentence with a 5-row example table (inputs → result, including one absent row) in the why panel, the same `exampleRows` the proposal card already has; have the `deriveColumn` recorder count absence per input (`absentBy: { population: 1204 }`) so the parenthetical is data, not a guess; render nested trees as an indented step list ('1. population absent? → absent; 2. cases ÷ population') rather than one sentence.

missing: Derived columns run over ALL rows and ignore the live selection — the design never says so, yet the NNDSS table mixes state, region and total roll-up rows, so an aggregate 'per-group total' silently double-counts unless the declaration can name which rows it runs over (an `over.where`) and the why sentence prints it.

`stampData` stamps only the DEFAULT table's version on every commit (session.ts:518-521), so a `column` commit on `jurisdictions` or `series`, or a derivation whose inputs come from a second table, is undated — 'derived against version X' cannot be answered for non-default tables until the stamp names every table the commit touches.

A formula edit or a same-name derivation on another branch changes derived VALUES without moving any table version, so `dataMoved` never fires for the commits that filtered on the old values — the stamp needs the derived columns' addresses (or the fold hash) beside the table versions.

The kernel tier of why() needs the derive flowchart's RuntimeSnapshot kept per (column, re-derivation run); after a refresh the old run's stages no longer produced the values on screen, and the design does not say which snapshot why() reaches or that it must say 'as re-derived at version Y'.

The session's `allMaterialized` / `materializedByCommit` are never pruned by `materialisedLost`, so after a refresh the gap sentence for a derived column reading a lost analysis column would name a column the engine no longer lists; likewise `overview().columns` needs the derived facets merged with their computed type, or `whats_here` shows the store's re-tallied type.

No persistence story for the data journal and for `DataSourceDef.derived` edits: a session replayed from an exported log needs the journal (refresh causes and re-derivation epochs) to derive staleness and dataMoved; the export format must carry both, or a replayed sheet misdates every derived header.

The `column` verb's proposal lane lets an agent propose a tree; nothing bounds the cost of evaluating an agent-proposed aggregate over 1M rows at proposal time (exampleRows on 'a sample' is stated, but the validator must also cap chain depth and refuse a proposal that reads a column the agent was not shown in whats_here — the Q8 boundary).

Cell-edit refusal is designed, but row-level `annotate` on a key is only possible for tables WITH a declared key; positional tables (the no-row-key law) have no addressable row, so the refusal's 'annotate row 4021' next action must itself be refused with a sentence on keyless tables.

Copy is described as a read that is not a commit, while the grids lens recommends recording it as a describe act; either is defensible, but a copied window carries the data version out of the tool (Ragavan/Bors: provenance must travel with the data) — the TSV should carry a header comment or a sidecar with table, version, filter and sort, or the pasted numbers are undated the moment they leave.

Column names: a derived column named the same as a future source column (a refresh adds `population` upstream) collides — the design refuses reserved and `~`-bearing names but not this; a refresh that arrives with a column whose name a derived column holds needs a typed gap (`derive-name-shadowed`) rather than the source silently winning or losing.
